videos.title: Random Dots Can Draw a Fractal #math #Shorts

editorial.opening: A finished fractal immediately poses the random-versus-structured puzzle.
editorial.mechanism: One moving point and its halfway image ground the corner-region map; the square contrast tests the rule.
editorial.readability: The dark plotting field separates the point cloud; a half label identifies the mapped point, and later anchors use dark ink.
editorial.pacing: The geometric explanation slows after the point buildup; second-level regions need inspection time.
editorial.sound: Dry proof narration with quiet original boundary notes. Full decode and ASR reviewed; no subjective listening or claim of pleasing prosody.
editorial.remaining_weaknesses: The infinite-set and burn-in caveats are verbal; a viewer unfamiliar with repeated maps may still need replay.
editorial.audience_evidence: Not measured. No retention, recognition, learning or subscription results yet.

videos.title: The Shortest Detour Is a Straight Line in Disguise #math #Shorts

editorial.opening: A movable riverbank touching point and live total length give a concrete minimization problem.
editorial.mechanism: Physical and reflected routes share P; equal lengths survive movement, and a straight unfolded route supplies the proof.
editorial.readability: A, B, B-prime and P are named. The total-length readout sits below the water, clear of captions.
editorial.pacing: The fold-back and equal-angle reveal are separated; a changed destination ends with a new optimizer.
editorial.sound: Dry proof narration with quiet original boundary notes. Full decode and ASR reviewed; no subjective listening or claim of pleasing prosody.
editorial.remaining_weaknesses: The line is an ideal straight bank, and the map remains schematic. No viewer test establishes whether the mirror argument is intuitive.

editorial.opening: The claim distinguishes a fair next toss from an unequal chance of reaching a boundary.
editorial.mechanism: A numbered token board stays linked to probability heights; the neighboring-average condition forces a line.
editorial.readability: The board uses dark numerals; the obsolete left/right arrows disappear before the starting point moves to three or five.
editorial.pacing: The averaging argument carries most of the cognitive load; this remains the most classroom-like episode.

videos.title: Where Did This Extra Hole Come From? #math #Shorts

editorial.opening: A rigid rearrangement reveals a real unit hole without removing a piece.
editorial.mechanism: Unequal slopes explain different boundaries; an explicitly magnified deviation inset shows their area difference.
editorial.readability: The inset names inward and outward deviations around a dashed straight baseline. Main pieces and hole retain grid outlines.
editorial.pacing: The initial rearrangement is quick, then repeated in both directions; the boundary comparison holds for the reasoning.
editorial.sound: Dry proof narration with quiet original boundary notes. Full decode and ASR reviewed; no subjective listening or claim of pleasing prosody.
editorial.remaining_weaknesses: The shallow 13-by-5 shape uses portrait space imperfectly; small slope differences rely on the labeled inset. No audience response is measured.
